title: "AI is becoming ordinary. The evidence about its effects is still catching up"
description: "As generative AI moves into classrooms and everyday life, the important scientific question is shifting from capability to effects."
date: 2026-09-22
image: "ai-use-mechanism.svg"

I was reading [OpenAI's call for research on AI and teen development](https://openai.com/index/teen-development-research-grants/) and one part of it stayed with me. The programme asks researchers to look at emotional development, relationships, patterns of use, safeguards, AI literacy and differences across social and cultural settings. That is a much more interesting set of questions than the one public discussion keeps returning to: is AI good or bad for learning?

On 8 September 2026, OpenAI announced $5 million for independent research on how generative AI affects people aged 13 to 17. The funding source obviously matters. A company developing the technology has an institutional interest in the evidence that develops around it, which makes independence, disclosure, publication and replication important. The programme at least acknowledges the issue by requiring conflict disclosures, including independence and credibility among its review criteria, and encouraging public release of findings.

What I like about the call is the implicit admission that "AI use" is not a very satisfactory exposure variable. Two students can spend thirty minutes with the same model and be doing almost opposite things. One can ask for an answer and copy it. The other can attempt the problem first, ask for criticism, argue with the response and revise the work. A study that records both as thirty minutes of AI use has measured time rather well and behaviour rather badly.

![The same amount of AI exposure can conceal very different learning behaviour.](ai-use-mechanism.svg){fig-alt="Thirty minutes of AI use branches into copying an answer or attempting a task, asking for feedback and revising." width="92%" fig-align="center"}

*Original schematic for EKO Perspectives.*

This is also why I am cautious about broad claims from early studies. A 2026 [meta-analysis in *Humanities and Social Sciences Communications*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-026-06903-y) reported generally positive pooled effects of generative-AI-supported approaches on outcomes including academic achievement, higher-order thinking and writing. That is useful evidence, but the pooled estimate is only the beginning of the interesting question. The intervention matters, as do the subject, the learner, the comparison group, study quality and the role the system actually played in the learning process.

There is a timing problem as well. The technology can change between study design and publication. Models improve, interfaces change, safeguards are added, and users learn new habits. A rigorous result can therefore become historically specific rather quickly. Social scientists are used to treatments changing in the real world, but generative AI compresses the timetable.

For universities and schools, I think this makes both the blanket ban and the blanket embrace difficult to defend from evidence alone. The useful questions are narrower. Does the system give feedback after a student has tried, or does it replace the attempt? Are we measuring exam performance, long-term retention, writing quality, confidence, critical reasoning or simply time saved? Do any gains remain when the tool is taken away? Are some students better placed than others to recognise a plausible but wrong answer?

These questions are less dramatic than asking whether AI will transform education, but they can actually be studied. The same problem will probably appear outside education too. A model can perform extremely well on a benchmark while producing a much less obvious effect once people reorganise their work around it. I suspect the interesting unit of analysis will increasingly be the human-machine arrangement rather than the model on its own.
